# Gospel of Philip — The HESED Reader's Guide
**Guide by:** HESED (חֶסֶד — Lovingkindness)

---

## At a Glance
| | |
|---|---|
| **Author** | Anonymous (attributed to Philip the Apostle; no direct connection) |
| **Date** | c. 180–250 CE (probably third century in its current form) |
| **Audience** | Members of the Valentinian Gnostic school, likely in Syria |
| **Genre** | Sacramental anthology / theological florilegium (collection of meditations) |
| **Timeline** | Third century, at the height of Valentinian Gnostic Christian influence |
| **In One Sentence** | A dense, poetic Valentinian Gnostic anthology meditating on five sacred sacraments — baptism, chrism, eucharist, redemption, and the bridal chamber — and on the mystery of Mary Magdalene's special relationship with Jesus, preserved in Coptic at Nag Hammadi. |

---

## The World Behind the Text

The Gospel of Philip is the most theologically sophisticated text in the Nag Hammadi library and one of the most challenging to read. It is not a gospel in any narrative sense — there is no story of Jesus's life, ministry, or death. It is a florilegium: a collection of loosely connected theological meditations, aphorisms, parables, and sacramental reflections that circle around a set of central Valentinian themes. The structure is associative rather than linear; ideas are connected by wordplay, imagery, and thematic resonance rather than by logical progression.

The text belongs to the Valentinian school of Gnostic Christianity — one of the most intellectually sophisticated movements of the second and third centuries. Valentinus himself (c. 100–175 CE) was a highly educated Christian teacher who taught in Rome, nearly became bishop of Rome by some accounts, and developed an elaborate theological system in which the material world arose from a crisis within the divine pleroma (fullness) and salvation consists in the restoration of divine sparks (pneumatics — spiritual people) to their divine origin. The Gospel of Philip represents a later stage of Valentinian thought, possibly from the Syrian wing of the school.

The world behind the text is one of intense liturgical and sacramental life. The Valentinians were not — as they are often caricatured — purely intellectual or anti-material. They had a rich sacramental practice, including a complex initiation rite called the "bridal chamber," which represented the mystic union of the soul with its divine counterpart (syzygy — paired angel). The Gospel of Philip is, among other things, a theological reflection on what these sacraments mean and do.

---

## Why This Book Was Written

The Gospel of Philip was written to articulate and defend a Valentinian theology of sacraments, salvation, and the nature of Christ. Its primary concerns are:

First, the sacraments. The text names five sacred rites: baptism, chrism (anointing), eucharist, redemption (apolytrosis), and the bridal chamber. Of these, the bridal chamber is the highest and most mystical — "the holy of the holy." Each sacrament is described with language that suggests both a physical rite and a spiritual reality that the physical rite points toward or participates in. The text insists on the necessity of the physical while consistently pointing beyond it: "The truth did not come into the world naked, but it came in types and images — the world will not receive truth in any other way."

Second, the nature of Christ. A famous saying: "The world came about through a mistake. For he who created it wanted to create it imperishable and immortal. He fell short of attaining his desire. For the world never was imperishable, nor, for that matter, was he who made the world." This is Valentinian demiurgology — the material world was created by a lesser divine being who lacked the full knowledge of the supreme God, and the resulting cosmos is flawed by that ignorance. This is not the creation of Genesis, which is pronounced "very good"; it is a creation born of failure.

Third, the role of Mary Magdalene. The Gospel of Philip contains the most extended treatment of Mary Magdalene in any Gnostic text, and the most famous passage: "[...] her more than [all] the disciples, and used to kiss her [often on her — lacuna —]. The rest of [the disciples...]. They said to him 'Why do you love her more than all of us?' The Savior answered and said to them, 'Why do I not love you like her?'" The physical lacuna — the hole in the papyrus where the object of the kiss was specified — is one of the most discussed gaps in all of early Christian scholarship.

---

## How to Read This Book

The Gospel of Philip cannot be read quickly. Its density and allusiveness demand slow, meditative engagement. Do not try to read it as a continuous argument — read it as a series of short, self-contained meditations that illuminate each other over time.

Several organizing themes will help orient you:

The light/darkness, truth/world opposition runs throughout. The material world is the realm of appearance and deception; the divine realm is the realm of truth and light. But Philip is careful: the material world is not evil in a simple Manichaean sense — it is necessary, it is the vehicle through which truth travels, it is valuable even if not ultimate.

The wordplay on Hebrew names is crucial and often untranslatable. The text opens with a meditation on how Hebrew names carry meaning that is lost in translation — those who say "God," "Father," "Son," "Holy Spirit," "Life," "Light," "Resurrection," and "Church" in their own language rather than in the original speak truth, while those who say them in Aramaic hear the names as sounds without meaning. This is a striking claim about the sacramental power of language.

The bridal chamber is the text's theological summit. It is the "holy of holies" into which only the anointed, the fully initiated, may enter. It represents the union of the soul with its divine counterpart — the restoration of the primordial syzygy that the fall disrupted. The language here is explicitly erotic (in the mystical tradition of the Song of Songs), and it may describe both a spiritual state and an actual ritual.

The famous passage about Mary Magdalene should be read carefully, with the lacuna honestly acknowledged. The most common reconstructions of the missing word are "mouth" or "lips" — "he kissed her on the mouth/lips." If this is correct, it is a physically intimate gesture that the male disciples resent. Jesus's response is to turn the question back: why do you not love me as I love her? The text implies that Mary's spiritual perception is deeper than that of the male disciples, and that the Savior's preference for her reflects this.

---

## The Threads — How This Book Connects

The five sacraments of Philip connect to the early Catholic tradition's development of the seven sacraments, but the Valentinian version is organized around a different logic: the hierarchy of sacraments leads upward from the external (baptism with water) through the internal (chrism with spirit) to the fully mystical (bridal chamber). This is an initiation system, more like the mystery religions of the Hellenistic world than the weekly liturgy of mainstream Christianity.

The demiurge theology — the material world created by mistake by a lesser divine being — connects to the broader Valentinian system described by Irenaeus in Against Heresies (c. 180 CE), to the Apocryphon of John, and to Ptolemy's Letter to Flora. Irenaeus's refutation of Valentinus, while polemical, is actually the best source for understanding what Valentinus taught, and it is worth reading alongside Philip.

Mary Magdalene's role connects to the Gospel of Mary, the Gospel of Thomas (saying 114), and the Pistis Sophia. Taken together, these texts construct a portrait of Mary as the pre-eminent disciple, the recipient of esoteric teaching, and the figure whose authority the male apostolic establishment most urgently resists.

The language of "types and images" for sacramental theology connects Philip to the Letter to the Hebrews (the Levitical system as a "shadow" of the heavenly reality), to Platonic philosophy (the visible world as a reflection of intelligible forms), and to the entire tradition of Christian sacramental theology, which has always wrestled with the relationship between the sign and what is signified.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

The most important thing to understand is that Philip is not anti-body. The Valentinian tradition is often caricatured as world-denying, but the Gospel of Philip insists that the resurrection is bodily: "Those who say that the Lord died first and (then) rose up are in error, for he rose up first and (then) died. If one does not first attain the resurrection, will he not die? As God lives, he would [already be dead]." The Valentinian resurrection is not escape from the body but the transformation of the body into a luminous, spiritual body — the "resurrection body" of 1 Corinthians 15:44.

The text's use of erotic imagery for spiritual union is deeply rooted in the Jewish tradition of reading the Song of Songs allegorically (as the love between God and Israel, or between Christ and the soul). Christian readers familiar with Bernard of Clairvaux's mystical commentaries on the Song of Songs will recognize the same impulse — the physical and the spiritual are not opposed but analogically related.

The critique of "those who call themselves Christians but know nothing of the mysteries" is insider polemic — the Valentinians regarded themselves as the pneumatics (spiritual Christians) who understood the inner meaning of the gospel, in contrast to psychics (soulish Christians, i.e., mainstream proto-orthodox Christians) who received only the surface teaching. Modern readers will find this hierarchy of spiritual insight deeply uncomfortable — but it was a common feature of mystery religion culture throughout the Hellenistic world, and the Valentinians were breathing that cultural air as much as they were breathing Christian air.

---

## Why This Book Isn't in Your Bible

The Gospel of Philip was never a candidate for the canon of the mainstream Christian movement. It was associated from its origin with the Valentinian school, which the proto-orthodox mainstream had been systematically refuting and excluding since the time of Irenaeus (c. 180 CE). By the fourth century, when canonical lists were being formalized, Valentinianism was a defeated and marginalized movement in most of the Roman world, and its texts were actively suppressed.

The survival of the Gospel of Philip (along with most of the Nag Hammadi library) almost certainly resulted from deliberate concealment — the books were hidden, probably by monks from the nearby Pachomian monastery of St. Pachomius, around the time (late fourth century) when Bishop Athanasius issued his canonical decree and began active suppression of non-canonical texts. They were hidden too well to be found for 1,600 years.

The Coptic translation (the only surviving version) dates from the fourth century; the Greek original may have been composed as early as the second century or as late as the mid-third. No major Christian tradition today includes Philip in its canon, though Gnostic revival movements and some feminist theologians have championed it as evidence of suppressed alternative Christianities.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|------|-------|
| c. 100–175 CE | Valentinus teaches in Rome; develops foundational Gnostic system |
| c. 180 CE | Irenaeus of Lyon writes Against Heresies, refuting Valentinianism |
| c. 200–250 CE | Gospel of Philip probably composed in Syrian Valentinian community |
| c. 300 CE | Coptic translation made |
| c. 367 CE | Athanasius issues canon list; Gnostic texts being suppressed |
| c. 390 CE | Estimated date of concealment of Nag Hammadi library |
| December 1945 CE | Nag Hammadi library discovered |
| 1959–1977 CE | Nag Hammadi texts gradually published; Philip fully edited by B. Layton |
| 2003 CE | Popular culture fixates on "Jesus kissed Mary" passage (Da Vinci Code) |
| 2000s–present | Scholarly debate continues on date, provenance, and sacramental system |

---
